# Biomechanics Framework for Injury Prediction and Rehabilitation

> Project By : Multidisciplinary AI Research Centre(MARC), University of Peradeniya

## Overview

This project implements an integrated wearable biomechanics system that unifies rigid-body mechanics with adaptive machine learning to monitor musculoskeletal health. By combining high-fidelity kinematic data from IMU sensor arrays with physics-informed neural networks, the system quantifies internal joint stresses and muscle tensions in real-time. **Key Features:**

* **Hybrid Inference Engine:** Integrates Newtonian inverse dynamics with deep learning (LSTM) to estimate individual muscle forces and joint reaction torques. * **Physics-Informed Modeling:** Grounded in musculoskeletal architecture and functional morphology to ensure biological plausibility in force estimations. * **Real-Time Injury Assessment:** Continuous monitoring of biomechanical "Failure Modes," including joint-angle asymmetry (>10°), muscle-force imbalance (>15%), and peak tension thresholds (e.g., >300N for tricep strain). **Hardware Support:**

* Designed for multi-node IMU configurations. ---

## Processing Pipeline & Notebooks

This repository includes a robust data processing pipeline consisting of three primary Jupyter notebooks. Each step is fully documented in the `Docs/` directory. ### 1. Dataset Manager (`01. Dataset Manager.ipynb`)

The dataset is managed via a central command interface bridging Google Drive and Google Colab, utilizing the `OpenDatasetStore` utility to maintain an automated JSON-indexed manifest of all experimental data. * **Entities (Subjects):** Participants are registered with unique IDs (e.g., `sub_0001`) along with their age, weight, height, and experience. * **Entries (Experiments):** Trials are logged as entries (e.g., `experiments_0001`) linked to specific subjects. Each experiment captures multi-modal data including raw IMU telemetry and synchronized video captures. * **Storage Architecture:** Data is neatly organized into `index/`, `raw_data/`, `related_files/`, and `processed_data/` directories. * **Further details:** Refer to [Docs/01. Dataset Documentation.md](<Docs/01.%20Dataset%20Documentation.md>)

### 2. Data Cleanup (`02. Data Cleanup.ipynb`)

The Data Cleaner serves as the preprocessing pipeline to extract, filter, and rename specific IMU sensor data for downstream kinematic analysis. * **Core Processing:** Identifies valid dataset columns using dynamic regular expressions (`get_columns`) and isolates primary telemetry axes (`extract_and_rename_imus`). * **Sensor Mapping:** Standardizes sensor node names based on hardware device IDs, producing anatomical labels like `RKP` (Right Knee Proximal), `REP` (Right Elbow Proximal), etc. * **Workflow:** Performs data ingestion, visual QA (via Plotly), optimal IMU extraction, and finally saves the subset data as `.parquet` files tagged `selected_for_4ang`. * **Further details:** Refer to [Docs/02. Data Cleanup.md](<Docs/02.%20Data%20Cleanup.md>)

### 3. Video Sync & 3-D Pose Estimation (`03. Video Sync.ipynb`)

This pipeline converts two unsynchronized RGB videos (front and side views) into a single, temporally coherent, root-centered 3-D skeletal sequence. * **2-D Keypoint Extraction:** Utilizes `yolo11x-pose` to detect 17 COCO keypoints per frame in each video. * **Temporal Synchronization:** Estimates frame lag between cameras using cross-correlation of a 1-D movement energy signal. * **Bayesian MAP 3-D Pose Fusion:** Solves for 3-D coordinates and global bone lengths iteratively via Batch EM. The objective function minimizes weighted reprojection error while enforcing an anatomical bone-length prior and temporal smoothness. * **Robust Optimization:** Uses `scipy.optimize.least_squares` with robust loss and sparse Jacobians to handle missing and noisy YOLO detections efficiently. * **Further details:** Refer to [Docs/03. Video Sync & 3‑D Pose Estimation.md](<Docs/03.%20Video%20Sync%20&%203%E2%80%91D%20Pose%20Estimation.md>)

## 1. Selecting Data for Joint Angle Estimation

The Wearable Biomechanics Data Cleaner serves as the preprocessing pipeline to extract, filter, and rename specific IMU sensor data for downstream kinematic analysis. It integrates directly with the `OpenDatasetStore` utility to transition data from raw formats into structured, processed entries. ### 1.1. Core Processing Functions

The pipeline relies on two primary Python functions that utilize dynamic regular expressions to isolate correct data streams

- **`get_columns(df, devices, imus, axes)`**: Identifies valid dataset columns by matching specified device IDs, IMU numbers, and spatial axes. It executes the regex pattern `^.*?(?<!\d){dev}_IMU{imu}_{axis}$` to ensure exact device number matching and prevent partial digit overlaps. - **`extract_and_rename_imus(df, imu_mapping)`**: Isolates the six primary telemetry axes (AX, AY, AZ, GX, GY, GZ) for designated sensors. It retains the underlying `Timestamp` data and reformats the column headers from their raw hardware IDs to target anatomical labels (e.g., yielding `RKP_AX`). ### 1.2. Standardized Sensor Mapping

Data extraction relies on a strict configuration dictionary that maps final target node names to specific hardware devices and their internal IMU indices. | **Target Node** | **Device ID** | Explaination                                      |
| --------------- | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| **RKP**         | 1             | Right Knee Proximal (Right leg, above the knee)   |
| **REP**         | 2             | Right Elbow Proximal (Right arm, above the elbow) |
| **LKP**         | 3             | Left Knee Proximal (Left leg, above the knee)     |
| **LEP**         | 4             | Left Elbow Proximal (Left arm, above the elbow)   |
| **RED**         | 6             | Right Elbow Distal (Right arm, below the elbow)   |
| **LED**         | 7             | Left Elbow Distal (Left arm, below the elbow)     |
| **LKD**         | 8             | Left Knee Distal (Left leg, below the knee)       |
| **RKD**         | 10            | Right Knee Distal (Right leg, below the knee)     |

### 1.3. Processing Workflow

1. **Initialization:** The script mounts Google Drive and points the `OpenDatasetStore` backend to `/content/drive/MyDrive/Datasets/Wearable-Biomechanics`. 2. **Data Ingestion:** Loads the raw dataset for a specified experiment entry (e.g., `experiments_0001`). 3. **Visual Quality Assurance:** Evaluates signal integrity by plotting data distributions (using violin and scatter plots via Plotly) for the active hardware devices. 4. **Extraction:** Passes the dataset through the `extract_and_rename_imus` function utilizing the established sensor mapping dictionary. In here from multiple IMUs in each device (IMU1, IMU2, IMU3) choose the best one, preferebly the the IMU in the device it self (IMU have the largest index IMU3 in 3 Sensor devices or IMU2 in 2 Sensor devices)

5. **Storage:** Commits the finalized, subset DataFrame to the `processed_data` directory within the store, appending the specific tag `selected_for_4ang` to the file.

## 1. Introduction & System Overview

This pipeline converts **two unsynchronized RGB videos** of a subject (a **front** view and a **side** view) into a **single temporally‑coherent, root‑centered 3‑D skeletal sequence** with consistent bone lengths across all frames. The pipeline is organized into four computational stages
```
┌────────────────┐     ┌────────────────┐
│  front.mp4     │     │  side.mp4      │
└────────┬───────┘     └────────┬───────┘
         │                      │
     [YOLO pose]           [YOLO pose]
         │                      │
         ▼                      ▼
  front_keypoints.json    side_keypoints.json
         │                      │
         └── cross‑correlate ───┘
                    │
                    ▼
            Δt  (side lag in frames)
                    │
          ┌─────────┴──────────┐
          ▼                    ▼
      synced front          synced side
          │                    │
          └─── Bayesian MAP ───┘
                    │
                    ▼
            X ∈ ℝ^(T × 17 × 3)
   fused confidence, global bone lengths
```

At a high level the algorithm,
1. Uses **YOLO11x‑pose** to detect 17 COCO keypoints per frame in each video. 2. Estimates the inter‑camera frame lag using **cross‑correlation of a 1‑D motion signal** derived from the keypoints. 3. Fuses the two synchronized 2‑D streams into 3‑D via a **batch Bayesian Maximum A Posteriori (MAP)** estimator solved with **SciPy `least_squares`** inside an **EM loop** that updates shared bone lengths. 4. Optionally renders skeleton‑annotated videos, a side‑by‑side synced video, and an interactive Plotly viewer comparing raw vs. reprojected 2‑D poses. ### 1.1. Environment & Data‑Store Setup

The notebook uses Google Colab and mounts the user's Google Drive. All artifacts are persisted through the **`OpenDatasetStore`** abstraction, which manages structured datasets under
```
/content/drive/MyDrive/Datasets/Wearable-Biomechanics/
```

|`entry_id_format`|`{type}_{num:04d}`|`experiments_0001`|
|`raw_filename_format`|`{entry_id}_{entity_id}_{ts}.csv`|—|

**Dependencies**

## 2. 2‑D Keypoint Extraction (YOLO Pose)

### 2.1. Model & Output

The pipeline uses `yolo11x-pose.pt`, the largest pose variant of Ultralytics YOLO11, which predicts
- A bounding box per person
- **17 COCO keypoints**, each with a pixel coordinate $(x, y)$ and confidence $c \in [0,1]$

The 17 keypoint indices (`KEYPOINT_NAMES`) are

| **idx** | **name**       | **idx** | **name**                                   |
| ------- | -------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| 0       | nose           | 9       | left_wrist                                 |
| 1       | left_eye       | 10      | right_wrist                                |
| 2       | right_eye      | 11      | **<font color="#f79646">left_hip</font>**  |
| 3       | left_ear       | 12      | <font color="#f79646">**right_hip**</font> |
| 4       | right_ear      | 13      | left_knee                                  |
| 5       | left_shoulder  | 14      | right_knee                                 |
| 6       | right_shoulder | 15      | left_ankle                                 |
| 7       | left_elbow     | 16      | right_ankle                                |
| 8       | right_elbow    |         |                                            |
Joints 11 and 12 (the hips) form the **root** and are treated specially during normalization. ### 2.2. Per‑Frame Extraction

For every frame `t` the pipeline records, 
$$\mathbf{p}_{j,t} \in \mathbb{R}^2, \quad c_{j,t} \in [0,1], \qquad j \in \{0,\dots,16\}$$
Missing detections are stored as `NaN` for coordinates and `0.0` for confidence, preserving the temporal grid so that `frame_idx` in the DataFrame directly corresponds to the physical frame number. ## 3. Temporal Synchronization of Multi‑View Video

Because the front and side cameras are started independently, their streams differ by an **unknown integer frame offset** $\Delta t$. We estimate this offset by aligning a scalar motion signal extracted from each view. ### 3.1. Motion Signal Construction

For each view, define a scalar per‑frame "movement energy"
$$m_t \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{17} \bigl\lVert \mathbf{p}_{j,t} - \mathbf{p}_{j,t-1} \bigr\rVert_2, \qquad t = 1, 2, \dots, T-1$$
**Intuition:** When the subject moves (jumps, squats, lifts), all 17 joints displace simultaneously $m_t$ spikes. During rest, $m_t$ drops near zero.

**Intuition:** When the subject moves (jumps, squats, lifts), all 17 joints displace simultaneously $m_t$ spikes. During rest, $m_t$ drops near zero. This creates a **characteristic 1‑D fingerprint** of the movement, dominated by gross body motion and independent of camera scale (since normalization follows). **Missing‑data handling:** If a joint's coordinates are `NaN`, the implementation duplicates the previous frame's coordinates so that no spurious spike is introduced,
$$\mathbf{p}_{j,t} \leftarrow \mathbf{p}_{j,t-1} \quad \text{if } \mathbf{p}_{j,t} \text{ is invalid}.$$

### 3.2. Standard Score Normalization

The two cameras observe the subject from very different distances, so the absolute magnitudes of $m_t$ differ. We normalize each signal to zero mean and unit variance

$$\hat{m}_t \;=\; \frac{m_t - \mu_m}{\sigma_m + 10^{-8}}$$
The small constant $10^{-8}$ avoids division by zero when the subject is perfectly still. ### 3.3. Cross‑Correlation & Lag Estimation

Define the cross‑correlation between the front and side normalized signals
$$C[\tau] \;=\; \sum_{t} \hat{m}^{\text{front}}[t] \, \hat{m}^{\text{side}}[t - \tau]$$
This is computed in one shot with `scipy.signal.correlate(front, side, mode='full')`, which yields valid lag,
$$\tau \in \{-(L_{\text{side}}-1), \dots, L_{\text{front}}-1\}.$$
The **optimal lag** is the correlation peak
$$\Delta t \;=\; \arg\max_{\tau} C[\tau]$$
**Interpretation:**
- $\Delta t > 0$ → the side stream **lags** the front by $\Delta t$ frames; the front video starts $\Delta t$ frames earlier. - $\Delta t < 0$ → the front stream lags the side by $\vert{}\Delta t\vert{}$ frames. - $\Delta t = 0$ → streams already aligned. The peak's **sharpness** reflects synchronization quality. a single dominant peak implies a confident estimate. ### 3.4. Applying the Lag

The lag is stored as `video_sync_side_lag_frames` on the experiment entry. During fusion, the sign is inverted (see §5.2) so that the two DataFrames begin at the same physical moment
$$\text{frame\_lag} = -\, \Delta t_{\text{stored}}.$$

Then
- If `frame_lag ≥ 0`, drop the first `frame_lag` rows of the **side** sequence. - If `frame_lag < 0`, drop the first `|frame_lag|` rows of the **front** sequence. - Trim to `min(len(front), len(side))` so both views have identical frame count. **Diagnostic Plots**
When `plot=True`, the routine renders two Plotly figures:
1. **Raw unsynchronized** normalized movement signals overlaid. 2. **Aligned** signals with the side stream shifted by `best_lag`, showing peak overlap. ## 4. Bayesian MAP 3‑D Pose Fusion

### 4.1. Coordinate Convention

After root‑centering and scale normalization the two views are interpreted as <font color="#f79646">**orthographic projections**</font> of the same 3‑D world

| **Camera** | **Observes 2‑D coordinate** | **World axis**                |
| ---------- | --------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Front      | $(u_f, v_f)$                | $X$ (lateral), $Y$ (vertical) |
| Side       | $(u_s, v_s)$                | $Z$ (depth), $Y$ (vertical)   |
Therefore
$$u_f \leftrightarrow X,\quad v_f \leftrightarrow Y,\quad u_s \leftrightarrow Z,\quad v_s \leftrightarrow Y.$$
Both cameras see the **same vertical axis $Y$**, which is the key redundancy that lets us constrain depth. ### 4.2. Pre‑processing Steps

**(a) Root centering.** For each frame $t$ define the root as the midpoint of the hips,
$$\mathbf{r}_t = \tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(\mathbf{p}_{11,t} + \mathbf{p}_{12,t}\right)$$
and shift every joint,
$$\mathbf{p}'_{j,t} = \mathbf{p}_{j,t} - \mathbf{r}_t.$$
If hip confidences drop below 0.1, fall back to the mean of all valid joints. The per‑frame root is stored for later reprojection. **(b) Per‑view scale normalization.** Median bone length over a fixed set of long reference bones,
$$\mathcal{B}_{\text{ref}} = \{\,(11,13),\,(12,14),\,(13,15),\,(14,16)\,\} \quad\text{(hip‑knee, knee‑ankle)}$$
$$s \;=\; \frac{1}{\mathrm{median}\bigl\{\, \lVert \mathbf{p}'_{a,t} - \mathbf{p}'_{b,t} \rVert \;:\; (a,b)\in\mathcal{B}_{\text{ref}},\; t \,\bigr\}}$$
Then every joint is scaled by $s$,
$$\mathbf{p}''_{j,t} = s \cdot \mathbf{p}'_{j,t}.$$
Because the reference bones are among the longest in the body, this normalizes both cameras to a **comparable anatomical unit** despite different focal lengths / distances. **(c) Validity masks.** A joint is considered valid when
$$\text{valid}_{j,t} = \neg\,\text{NaN}(\mathbf{p}_{j,t}) \;\wedge\; c_{j,t} > 0.05.$$
### 4.3. The MAP Objective
Let the latent variables be
- $X_t \in \mathbb{R}^{17 \times 3}$ — the 3‑D joint positions at frame $t$
- $L_b \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ — the global bone length for each skeleton pair $b$

The joint cost function (negative log‑posterior) is,
  $$E(X, L) \;=\; E_{\text{reproj}} \;+\; \lambda_{\text{bone}} \, E_{\text{bone}} \;+\; \lambda_{\text{temp}} \, E_{\text{temp}} $$
#### 4.3.1.

$

The joint cost function (negative log‑posterior) is,
  $$E(X, L) \;=\; E_{\text{reproj}} \;+\; \lambda_{\text{bone}} \, E_{\text{bone}} \;+\; \lambda_{\text{temp}} \, E_{\text{temp}} $$
#### 4.3.1. Weighted Reprojection Error
$$E_{\text{reproj}} \;=\; \sum_{t}\sum_{j} c_{j,t}\, \Bigl[\,(X_{j,t}^x - u^f_{j,t})^2 + (X_{j,t}^y - v^f_{j,t})^2 + (X_{j,t}^z - u^s_{j,t})^2 + (X_{j,t}^y - v^s_{j,t})^2 \,\Bigr]$$
Notice

- The **front view** constrains $X$ and $Y$. - The **side view** constrains $Z$ and the same $Y$. - The vertical coordinate $Y$ appears in **both** terms, coupling the two views. Because the residuals are multiplied by $\sqrt{c_{j,t}}$ inside `least_squares`, the squared objective is scaled by $c_{j,t}$ — YOLO‑confident joints are trusted more. #### 4.3.2. Anatomical Bone‑Length Prior
$$E_{\text{bone}} \;=\; \sum_{t}\sum_{(p_1,p_2) \in \text{Pairs}} \Bigl(\, \bigl\lVert X_{p_1,t} - X_{p_2,t} \bigr\rVert_2 \;-\; L_b \,\Bigr)^2$$
This enforces that a bone's Euclidean length in 3‑D matches a **single global estimate** $L_b$ across all frames. It is the primary constraint that resolves the $Z$ ambiguity: without it, many $(X,Y,Z)$ combinations would reproject to the same 2‑D points. **Skeleton pairs** (COCO 17)
  $$\{(0,1),(0,2),(1,3),(2,4),(5,6),(5,7),(7,9),(6,8),(8,10),(5,11),(6,12),(11,12),(11,13),(13,15),(12,14),(14,16)\}$$
#### 4.3.3. Temporal Smoothness (Constant‑Velocity Prior)
$$E_{\text{temp}} \;=\; \sum_{t=2}^{T}\sum_{j=1}^{17} \bigl\lVert X_{j,t} - 2X_{j,t-1} + X_{j,t-2} \bigr\rVert^2$$
This is the squared **second finite difference** — i.e., acceleration — and penalizes physically implausible high‑frequency jitter. It does not bias smooth, low‑acceleration motions. #### 4.3.4. Total Weighted Residual Vector
`least_squares` minimizes $\tfrac12\lVert f(\mathbf{X}) \rVert^2$, so we pass the square roots of the weights:

  

$$f(\mathbf{X}) = \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{c}\,(X^x - u^f) \\ \sqrt{c}\,(X^y - v^f) \\ \sqrt{c}\,(X^z - u^s) \\ \sqrt{c}\,(X^y - v^s) \\ \sqrt{\lambda_{\text{temp}}}\,(X_t - 2X_{t-1} + X_{t-2}) \\ \sqrt{\lambda_{\text{bone}}}\,(\lVert X_{p_1}-X_{p_2}\rVert - L_b) \end{bmatrix}$$
so that $\tfrac12\lVert f\rVert^2 = \tfrac12(E_{\text{reproj}} + \lambda_{\text{bone}} E_{\text{bone}} + \lambda_{\text{temp}} E_{\text{temp}})$. ### 4.4. Optimization Strategy - Batch EM

Bone lengths are unknown a priori, so we alternate between two steps,

**E‑step (Solve poses, fix $L$)**
Solve for all $T \cdot 17 \cdot 3$ coordinates with `scipy.optimize.least_squares`

|**Setting**|**Rationale**|
|---|---|
|`method='trf'`|Trust Region Reflective — bounded, stable, sparse‑friendly|
|`loss='soft_l1'`|Huber‑like robust loss; down‑weights outlier YOLO detections|
|`f_scale=5.0`|Residual scale above which the loss becomes linear|
|`x_scale='jac'`|Auto‑scaled variables for numerical conditioning|
|`jac_sparsity`|Custom CSR pattern → sparse finite differences|

**M‑step (Update bones, fix $X$)**
Recompute each bone's global length as the **median** of its measured length over all frames:

$$L_b \;\leftarrow\; \operatorname{median}_{t}\Bigl\lVert X_{p_1,t} - X_{p_2,t} \Bigr\rVert$$
Median (rather than mean) adds robustness to outlier frames. **Convergence** 
For each EM iteration the change $\Delta L = \max_b \vert{}L_b^{(k)} - L_b^{(k-1)}\vert{}$ is printed. With `n_em_iters = 3` the pipeline converges in practice. ### 4.5. Jacobian Sparsity Matrix

A naive dense Jacobian would have shape $(4TJ + 3(T-2)J + TP)\times(3TJ)$, which grows extremely fast. Because each residual only touches a handful of unknowns, we build a sparse CSR mask with the exact nonzero pattern:

|**Residual block**|**Rows**|**Nonzero columns per row**|
|---|---|---|
|Front‑X|$TJ$|1 (`X^x`)|
|Front‑Y|$TJ$|1 (`X^y`)|
|Side‑Z|$TJ$|1 (`X^z`)|
|Side‑Y|$TJ$|1 (`X^y`)|
|Temporal|$3(T-2)J$|3 (frame $t,t\!-\!1,t\!-\!2$)|
|Bone|$TP$|6 ($p_1,p_2$ × 3 coords)|

Total rows,
$$n_{\text{res}} = 4TJ + 3(T-2)J + TP.$$
Total parameters,
$$n_{\text{par}} = 3TJ.$$
This typically delivers **one to two orders of magnitude** speed‑up in finite‑difference Jacobian evaluation. ### 4.6. Initialization

**(a) 3‑D seed $X_0$**
$$X_0^x = u^f,\qquad X_0^z = u^s,\qquad X_0^y = \frac{w_f\, v^f + w_s\, v^s}{w_f + w_s + \epsilon},$$
where $w_f, w_s$ are validity masks. The $Y$ blend ensures joints seen by only one camera still receive a sensible vertical estimate. **(b) Bone seed $L_b^{(0)}$**
$$L_b^{(0)} = \max\Bigl(\, \operatorname{median}_t \lVert X_{p_1,t}-X_{p_2,t}\rVert^{(f)},\; \operatorname{median}_t \lVert X_{p_1,t}-X_{p_2,t}\rVert^{(s)} \,\Bigr)$$
i.e., the larger of the two single‑view medians. Taking the max avoids under‑estimating depth‑projected foreshortened bones. ### 4.7. Confidence Fusion

For each joint, the fused confidence is the clipped sum of the two view confidences
$$c^{\text{fused}}_{j,t} \;=\; \mathrm{clip}\!\left(c^f_{j,t} + c^s_{j,t},\; 0,\; 1\right)$$
with joints unseen in either view set to 0. ### 4.8.

fidence is the clipped sum of the two view confidences
$$c^{\text{fused}}_{j,t} \;=\; \mathrm{clip}\!\left(c^f_{j,t} + c^s_{j,t},\; 0,\; 1\right)$$
with joints unseen in either view set to 0. ### 4.8. Inverse Scaling to Output Units

Finally, the internal normalized 3‑D points are converted back to **front‑view pixel units** via,
$$X^{\text{out}} = X_{\text{opt}} \cdot \frac{1}{s_f},\qquad L^{\text{out}}_b = L_b \cdot \frac{1}{s_f}.$$
Storing one consistent scale lets the visualization reproject both views using the fixed ratio,
$$\rho = \frac{s_f}{s_s}.$$

|**Output**|**Shape**|**Meaning**|
|---|---|---|
|`fused_3d_pts`|$(T, 17, 3)$|Root‑centered 3‑D joints, front‑pixel units|
|`fused_scores`|$(T, 17)$|Fused confidence per joint|
|`final_bones`|$(P,)$|Global bone lengths in front‑pixel units|

## 5. Parameter Reference & Tuning Guide

| **Parameter**                                          | **Default** | **Effect**                                                                                 | **When to change**                                              |

## 6. Assumptions, Failure Modes, and Limitations

### 6.1. Assumptions

1. **Orthographic projection.** Both cameras are modeled as orthographic. Perspective distortion is ignored. For a subject > 3 m away from the camera, error is small; for close‑ups, significant foreshortening must be corrected with a proper camera calibration. 2. **Axis‑aligned cameras.** The front camera's optical axis is assumed to lie along the world $Z$, and the side camera's along the world $X$. Oblique camera placement will rotate the recovered 3‑D cloud relative to the true world frame. 3. **Rigid skeleton.** All bone lengths are constant across the trial. Growing subjects, soft‑tissue artifacts, or compression apparel will violate this. 4. **Single person in frame.** YOLO returns the first detected pose, multiple people in the frame will mix skeletons. 5. **At least 3 frames** are required for the temporal smoothness term. ### 6.2. An fPCA score (Functional Principal Component Analysis score) serves a completely different purpose than SPARC or LDLJ-A. While SPARC and LDLJ-A calculate a single, explicit index for movement smoothness, fPCA is a data-driven statistical technique used to capture and quantify the dominant modes of variation across an entire movement curve. [1, 2, 3]

Instead of focusing only on "jerkiness," an fPCA score tells you how much and in what specific way an individual's movement trajectory deviates from the average population curve. [4]

---

## 1. How the fPCA Score Works

Think of standard PCA as extracting patterns from static columns of numbers. fPCA extracts patterns from continuous time-series curves (like a velocity profile over time, or hip/knee angles during a stride). [1, 5]

1. The Mean Curve: fPCA computes the average trajectory across all subjects/trials. [6]
2. Functional Principal Components (fPCs): It extracts characteristic "modes of variation" (curves, not single numbers) that explain where the data varies the most. [1, 4]
3. The Score: For any individual trial, the fPCA score is a weight (a single number) indicating how strongly that specific trial matches a given fPC curve. [3, 4]

Mathematically, an individual movement curve $X_i(t)$ is reconstructed as:  
$$X_i(t) \approx \mu(t) + \text{score}_{i,1}\psi_1(t) + \text{score}_{i,2}\psi_2(t) + \dots$$

- μ(t) = Mean curve of the population. - $\psi_k(t)$ = The k-th functional component (the pattern shape). - $\text{score}_{i,k}$ = The fPCA score (how much of that pattern this individual exhibits). [4, 6]

---

## 2. Biomechanical Meaning of fPCA Scores

An fPCA score allows researchers to turn complex, multi-second movement graphs into simple coordinates for clinical analysis: [2]

- Score = 0: The subject's movement perfectly mirrors the average shape of the group. [7]
- Positive vs. Negative Scores: Indicate opposite physical deviations from the norm. - _Example:_ If ψ₁(t) represents an early peak in velocity, a high positive score means the subject accelerated aggressively early on. A negative score means they accelerated much later than average. [8]
    

---

## 3. Comparison: SPARC vs. LDLJ-A vs. fPCA Score

|Feature|SPARC / LDLJ-A|fPCA Score|
|---|---|---|
|Primary Goal|Direct evaluation of smoothness.|Mapping overall coordination variability.|
|Output Type|Fixed clinical score (e.g., -1.5 is always smooth).|Data-dependent weight (relative to the dataset).|
|What it Captures|Micro-fluctuations, tremors, and jerks.|Macro-shape shifts, timing delays, and amplitude changes.|
|Interpretation|Absolute (higher is always better).|Relative (positive/negative depend entirely on the pattern).|

## 4. Can fPCA be used to measure smoothness? Yes, but indirectly. # Offline Two-Pass Calibration + EKF Pipeline for Knee Angle Estimation

Yes — this is actually the **ideal approach** for biomechanics research. Since you're not constrained by real-time processing, you can use the entire dataset to extract high-quality calibration parameters, then run the EKF with those parameters **fixed**. This is standard practice in gait analysis and gives you far better results than trying to estimate everything online. The workflow has two distinct passes:

---

## 1. Pass 1: Calibration (Data-Driven Parameter Extraction)

In this pass, you extract all the time-invariant parameters that the EKF needs. You do **not** run the filter yet. ### 1.1. Static Bias Calibration

If your dataset starts with a **static standing period** (common in gait datasets — subject stands still for 5–10 seconds before running):

- **Gyro bias:** Average the gyro readings during the static period. $$
  \hat{\mathbf{b}}_{g,T} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N} \boldsymbol{\omega}_{m,T,k}, \quad \hat{\mathbf{b}}_{g,S} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N} \boldsymbol{\omega}_{m,S,k}
  $$
- **Accel bias:** If you have a known reference orientation, you can estimate accel bias. If not, assume it's zero (most MEMS accelerometers are factory-calibrated for bias, and running datasets often pre-calibrate this). - **Initial orientation:** Use the static period's accelerometer reading to compute initial roll and pitch (gravity direction). If a magnetometer is available, use it for initial yaw; otherwise set yaw to zero. If there's **no static period**, you can still estimate gyro bias from the **stance phase** of running. During mid-stance (foot flat on ground), the shank angular velocity is near zero for a brief window. Detect these windows using a threshold on gyro magnitude and average across many steps. ### 1.2. Joint Axis Estimation (The Key Calibration)

This is the most important calibration step. The knee's hinge axis in the **thigh IMU frame** (\( \mathbf{r}_T \)) and in the **shank IMU frame** (\( \mathbf{r}_S \)) can be estimated from the data without any optical reference. **Method: Relative Angular Velocity Parallelism**

The principle: during pure knee flexion/extension, the relative angular velocity between shank and thigh is aligned with the joint axis. Even during running, the dominant motion is flexion/extension, so the relative angular velocity vectors will cluster around the joint axis. **Algorithm:**

1. Compute the relative angular velocity in the thigh frame at each time step:
$$
   \mathbf{m}_k = \mathbf{R}_{T,k}^T \mathbf{R}_{S,k} (\boldsymbol{\omega}_{m,S,k} - \hat{\mathbf{b}}_{g,S}) - (\boldsymbol{\omega}_{m,T,k} - \hat{\mathbf{b}}_{g,T})
$$
   Note: for this step, you need orientation estimates. You can get rough orientations by running a **simple complementary filter** or even just integrating the gyro over short windows. The joint axis estimation is robust to moderate orientation errors because it relies on the *direction* of \( \mathbf{m}_k \), not its magnitude. 2. Stack all relative angular velocity vectors into a matrix:
$$
   \mathbf{M} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{m}_1 & \mathbf{m}_2 & \cdots & \mathbf{m}_N \end{bmatrix}^T \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}
$$

3. Perform **Principal Component Analysis (PCA)** or **Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)** on \( \mathbf{M} \). The first principal component (the direction of maximum variance) is the joint axis in the thigh frame:
$$
   \hat{\mathbf{r}}_T = \text{first column of } \mathbf{V} \text{ from } \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{U} \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \mathbf{V}^T
$$
   The sign is arbitrary; fix it by ensuring \( \hat{\mathbf{r}}_T \) points in a consistent direction (e.g., from medial to lateral, or such that knee flexion is positive). 4. Transform to the shank frame using the mean relative rotation:
$$
   \hat{\mathbf{r}}_S = \bar{\mathbf{R}}_{TS} \hat{\mathbf{r}}_T
$$
   where $\bar{\mathbf{R}}_{TS}$ is the average relative rotation over the dataset. **Why this works:** During running, the knee undergoes large flexion/extension (the dominant motion), so the relative angular velocity is mostly along the hinge axis. The orthogonal components (from soft-tissue artifact, sensor noise, and small out-of-plane motion) are much smaller and get averaged out by PCA. **Refinement:** You can iteratively refine the axis. After the first EKF run, re-estimate the axis using the filter's orientation estimates (which are more accurate), then re-run the EKF. This is a **two-iteration** approach that converges quickly. ### 1.3. Sensor-to-Segment Alignment (Optional but Recommended)

If you have a **functional calibration movement** in the dataset (e.g., a slow knee bend, a squat, or a known pose), you can estimate the rotation from the IMU frame to the anatomical segment frame. For running specifically, you can use the **static standing period** to align the IMU's vertical axis with the anatomical vertical (gravity).

The joint axis estimation (Section 1.2) gives you the medial-lateral axis. The cross product gives you the third axis:

\[
\mathbf{a}_{\text{vertical}} = \text{gravity direction in IMU frame (from accel)}

\]

These three axes form the sensor-to-segment rotation matrix. ### 1.4. Noise Covariance Estimation

From the static period (or quiet stance phases):

- **Gyro noise \( \sigma_g^2 \):** Variance of the gyro readings during static periods. - **Accel noise \( \sigma_a^2 \):** Variance of the accelerometer readings during static periods. - **Gyro bias random walk \( \sigma_{bg}^2 \):** Estimated from the Allan variance of the gyro during static periods, or set to a small value. - **Constraint noise \( \mathbf{R}_c \):** Set based on the expected soft-tissue artifact. A good starting point is \( \sigma_c = 0.05\text{--}0.2 \) rad/s, tuned by looking at the residual during the calibration movement. ---

## 2. Pass 2: EKF with Fixed Calibration

Now you run the EKF with all the parameters from Pass 1 **fixed**. You can choose to:

- **Fix the joint axis** \( \hat{\mathbf{r}}_T \) (recommended if you're confident in the calibration). - **Fix the gyro biases** (recommended if you have a good static period). - **Still estimate** the attitude errors and possibly small residual bias corrections. ### 2.1. Simplified State Vector

If you fix the joint axis and biases, the error state reduces to just the two attitude errors:

\[
\delta \mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} \delta \boldsymbol{\theta}_T \\ \delta \boldsymbol{\theta}_S \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^6
\]

This is a **huge simplification** — the covariance is 6×6 instead of 15×15, and the Jacobians are much smaller. The filter is faster and more stable. If you want to allow small bias corrections (recommended), keep the bias errors in the state:

\[
\delta \mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} \delta \boldsymbol{\theta}_T \\ \delta \boldsymbol{\theta}_S \\ \delta \mathbf{b}_{g,T} \\ \delta \mathbf{b}_{g,S} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{12}
\]

But **fix the joint axis** (remove \( \delta \mathbf{r}_T \) from the state). This is the sweet spot for offline processing: you get bias adaptation without the complexity of estimating the joint axis online. ### 2.2. Measurement Updates

Run the EKF with:

1. **Accelerometer updates** (gravity reference) at each time step for both IMUs. 2. **Joint axis constraint updates** at each time step using the fixed \( \hat{\mathbf{r}}_T \). The constraint Jacobian simplifies because \( \delta \mathbf{r}_T = 0 \):

\[
\mathbf{H}_c = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{P} [\hat{\mathbf{R}}_{TS} \boldsymbol{\omega}_S']_\times & -\mathbf{P} \hat{\mathbf{R}}_{TS} [\boldsymbol{\omega}_S']_\times & \mathbf{P} & -\mathbf{P} \hat{\mathbf{R}}_{TS} \end{bmatrix}
\]

where \( \mathbf{P} = I - \hat{\mathbf{r}}_T \hat{\mathbf{r}}_T^T \) is the projection orthogonal to the fixed joint axis. ### 2.3. Optional: Smoothing Pass

Since you're offline, you can run a **Rauch-Tung-Striebel (RTS) smoother** after the forward EKF pass. This runs the filter backward in time and produces smoothed estimates that are more accurate than the forward-only filter. This is a standard technique in offline biomechanics and can reduce errors by 20–40%. The RTS smoother equations:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{C}_k &= \mathbf{P}_{k|k} \Phi_k^T \mathbf{P}_{k+1|k}^{-1} \\
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|N} &= \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k} + \mathbf{C}_k (\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k+1|N} - \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k+1|k}) \\
\mathbf{P}_{k|N} &= \mathbf{P}_{k|k} + \mathbf{C}_k (\mathbf{P}_{k+1|N} - \mathbf{P}_{k+1|k}) \mathbf{C}_k^T
\end{aligned}
\]

For the error-state formulation, the smoother operates on the error state and covariance, then the smoothed errors are injected into the nominal state. ---

## 4. Practical Tips for Offline Processing

1. **Don't over-engineer the filter.** With good calibration from Pass 1, the EKF in Pass 2 can be simple. Fix the joint axis and biases; only estimate attitude errors. This is more robust than trying to estimate everything online. 2. **Validate the joint axis calibration.** After Pass 1, check that the residual \( \mathbf{e} = \mathbf{m} - (\mathbf{m} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{r}}_T)\hat{\mathbf{r}}_T \) is small during knee flexion/extension. If it's not, the axis is wrong — try a different calibration movement or refine with more data. 3. **Use the RTS smoother.** For offline biomechanics, there's no reason not to. It's a few extra lines of code and gives significantly better joint angle estimates, especially at the start and end of the dataset where the forward filter hasn't fully converged. 4. **Iterate once.** Run the EKF, then use the filtered orientations to re-estimate the joint axis (Pass 1, step 5), then re-run the EKF. This two-iteration approach typically converges to the optimal axis. 5. **Check the innovation sequence.** Plot the constraint innovation \( \mathbf{v}_k = -\mathbf{e}_k \) over time. It should be zero-mean and white if the filter is consistent. If it has a bias, your joint axis is slightly off. If it's correlated, your noise covariances are wrong. 6. **Time synchronization.** If the two IMUs are separate devices, ensure their timestamps are aligned. A time offset of even 10 ms can cause significant errors in the relative angular velocity during running. If you have a common trigger or sync signal, use it. Otherwise, estimate the offset by cross-correlating the gyro signals during a known event (e.g., foot strike). 7. **Handle the first few seconds carefully.** The EKF needs a few steps to converge. Discard the first 1–2 seconds of output, or initialize the covariance large and let it settle. ---

This two-pass approach gives you the best of both worlds: the calibration quality of a batch optimization and the robustness of a recursive filter. It's the standard methodology in offline gait analysis, and it will give you knee angle estimates accurate to within a few degrees without any magnetometer.

Extracting reliable 3D joint angles from asynchronous, multi-view 2D video requires a pipeline that handles markerless pose estimation, signal-based temporal synchronization, and stereo triangulation. This approach avoids manual frame matching and leverages established computer vision algorithms validated against optical marker systems. **1.2D Pose Extraction:**Run independently on both unaligned videos. Process both the front and side videos through a scientifically validated markerless pose estimation framework. - **OpenPose** or **MediaPipe (BlazePose)** are the standard choices in biomechanics literature for tracking anatomical landmarks. - Extract the $(u, v)$ pixel coordinates for all major joints (hips, knees, ankles, shoulders, elbows) for every frame. Save these as separate time-series datasets. Do not worry about the frame mismatch yet. **2.Temporal Synchronization:**Aligning the time-series via cross-correlation. Instead of manually guessing the visual sync point, use the kinematic data itself to find the exact frame offset. - Select a fast-moving joint with a clear trajectory in both views (e.g., the vertical $y$-coordinate of the ankle during a foot strike, or the wrist during a swing). - Compute the cross-correlation between the front-view 1D signal and the side-view 1D signal (e.g., using `scipy.signal.correlate` in Python). - The peak of the cross-correlation function represents the exact frame lag ($\Delta t$) between the two cameras. Trim the arrays so both datasets start and end on the exact same synchronized frame. **3.3D Trajectory Reconstruction:**Triangulating coordinates using Direct Linear Transformation (DLT). To convert the synchronized 2D pixel pairs into real-world 3D coordinates $(X, Y, Z)$, you must establish the spatial relationship between the cameras. - If you recorded a checkerboard calibration pattern, compute the intrinsic and extrinsic camera matrices. - If uncalibrated, identify at least 6 known static reference points visible in both the front and side views (corners of a room, a marked calibration wand) to compute the Direct Linear Transformation (DLT) matrix. - Pass the synchronized 2D points and your projection matrices into a triangulation function (like `cv2.triangulatePoints`) to yield raw 3D spatial coordinates for each joint over time. **4.Joint Angle Computation:**Vector mathematics and anatomical filtering. Define the body segments as 3D vectors. For example, the thigh vector is defined from the hip to the knee, and the shank vector from the knee to the ankle. - Use the dot product and cross product of these adjacent segment vectors to calculate the raw anatomical joint angles (flexion/extension, abduction/adduction). - Because vision-based tracking introduces high-frequency noise, pass the computed angles through a zero-lag 4th-order Butterworth low-pass filter (cutoff frequency typically between 6 Hz and 10 Hz for human motion). Alternatively, if you are fusing this vision data with IMU kinematics, feed these 3D positions directly into an Error-State Kalman Filter (ESKF) as your observation update to smooth the final angle estimation.
